chunks: Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Faddal from Amr ibn Sa'id from Musaddiq ibn Sadah from Ammar ibn Musa from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

I asked him about a man who sets out for a need and travels five or six farasikh, then arrives at a village and stays there, then leaves it and travels another five or six farasikh; is that permissible? He said: 'He is not considered a traveler until he travels eight farasikh from his home or village, so he should perform the complete prayer (salat al-tamam).'

Because this narration is restricted to one who left his house without the intention of travel, so his journey extended until he became a traveler without intention; thus, complete prayer is obligatory upon him. Even if the distance reached what would require shortening (qasr) if he had intended it, complete prayer is obligatory upon him only because he did not intend a journey of the specific measure that requires shortening. And what supports this interpretation is what was narrated:

key_terms.التَّقْصِيرُ: Al-taqseer, the shortening of the four-rak'at prayer to two rak'ats for travelers.
key_terms.التَّمَامُ: Al-tamam, the complete prayer (four rak'ats) as opposed to the shortened prayer.
key_terms.فَرَاسِخ: Frasakh (plural of farasikh), a unit of distance used in Islamic jurisprudence for determining travel distance.
key_terms.مُسَافِراً: Musafiran, a traveler entitled to specific legal concessions such as shortening prayers.
key_terms.نِيَّةُ السَّفَرِ: Niyyat al-safar, the intention of travel, a key condition for certain legal rulings.

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on prayer for someone who travels a long distance without initially intending to be a traveler?
ai.summary: This narration from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies the distinction between a traveler who sets out with the intent to travel versus one who merely extends their journey, ruling that the latter must perform complete prayers (tamam) until covering eight farasikh. Shaykh al-Tusi highlights that this ruling applies specifically to those who did not initially intend a journey of the required distance, emphasizing the role of intention (niyyah) in determining the status of musafir. This distinction ensures that the concession of qasr is not applied to those who merely happen to be away from home without the requisite travel intent.
